title: Week 21 · Lesson 45: Dermatologic Pharmacology — Eczema, Acne, Psoriasis, Skin Infection & Medication Safety
html:
PHASE 2 · ADVANCED PHARMACOLOGY

Week 21 — Lesson 45: Dermatologic Pharmacology — Eczema, Acne, Psoriasis, Skin Infection & Medication Safety

FNP-level goal: Match dermatologic medication to a defensible diagnosis, lesion morphology, body site, severity, infection risk, and patient-specific safety factors—while recognizing the rashes, infections, and drug reactions that need urgent evaluation or specialty care.

Learning Objectives

  • Use morphology, distribution, time course, exposures, and systemic symptoms before choosing a skin medication.
  • Apply topical corticosteroid and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory therapy safely by site, potency, duration, and diagnosis.
  • Build an acne plan that combines mechanisms and avoids unnecessary antibiotic exposure.
  • Distinguish inflammatory dermatoses from bacterial, fungal, viral, and severe drug-related skin disease.
  • Recognize red flags requiring urgent evaluation, procedural care, or dermatology referral.

Part 1 — A Rash Is a Clinical Problem, Not a Topical-Steroid Diagnosis

Before prescribing, define what is on the skin: macule, papule, plaque, vesicle, pustule, scale, crust, erosion, ulcer, purpura, or nodule. Then ask where it is, how fast it changed, whether it itches or hurts, whether there is fever or mucosal involvement, and whether there are new medications, contacts, travel, animal exposure, occupational exposures, or immune compromise.

Topical medication can suppress inflammation and temporarily change appearance. That can be helpful when the diagnosis is sound and harmful when it masks infection, delays a biopsy, worsens an untreated fungal process, or reassures a patient with a severe drug reaction. Diagnosis and disposition come before the tube.

Part 2 — Topical Corticosteroids: Powerful by Design

Topical corticosteroids are commonly used for inflammatory dermatoses such as atopic dermatitis and selected contact dermatitis presentations. Choose potency, vehicle, quantity, body site, duration, age, skin integrity, and diagnosis carefully. Thin skin and high-absorption areas—such as face, eyelids, intertriginous areas, and genitals—require especially cautious selection.

Adverse effects can include skin atrophy, striae, telangiectasia, acneiform eruption, pigment change, and systemic absorption in higher-risk use. “It is only topical” is not a complete safety assessment. Document where, how often, how long, and when the patient should stop and return.

Part 3 — Eczema: Repair the Barrier and Control Inflammation

Atopic dermatitis management includes regular moisturization, trigger reduction, anti-inflammatory treatment for flares, itch/sleep assessment, and surveillance for secondary infection. The treatment target is not simply a less-red rash; it is restored barrier function, improved sleep/function, and fewer flares with the least treatment burden that works.

Topical calcineurin inhibitors and other nonsteroidal options can be useful in selected cases, especially when steroid-sparing treatment is appropriate. Avoid treating eczema with routine topical antimicrobials or systemic corticosteroids as a default long-term strategy. Escalating disease, recurrent infection, extensive involvement, or uncertain diagnosis warrants reassessment and possible dermatology support.

Part 4 — Infection Can Mimic Eczema, and Eczema Can Invite Infection

Oozing, honey-colored crust, rapidly worsening pain, warmth, fever, pustules, or systemic symptoms change the differential. Consider bacterial infection, herpes-related disease, fungal infection, scabies, or another process rather than repeatedly increasing anti-inflammatory treatment.

Patients with extensive painful erosions, eye involvement, fever, or rapidly progressive lesions need urgent evaluation. Do not tell a systemically ill patient with a rapidly changing rash to wait for a topical medication to “start working.”

Part 5 — Acne: Use Multiple Mechanisms, Not Endless Antibiotics

Acne management may include topical retinoids, benzoyl peroxide, topical antibiotics, azelaic acid, hormonal options, and selected systemic therapies according to lesion type, severity, scarring risk, pregnancy potential, prior response, and patient preference. Mild comedonal disease, inflammatory papules/pustules, nodulocystic disease, and acneiform drug eruption are not the same condition.

Current acne guidance supports combining mechanisms and limiting antibiotic exposure. When topical or oral antibiotics are used, benzoyl peroxide and other appropriate topical therapy help reduce resistance risk. A repeated isolated antibiotic refill without an acne assessment is not stewardship.

Part 6 — Acne Medication Safety

Ask about skin irritation, sun exposure, concurrent products, pregnancy possibility, menstrual or androgen-related symptoms, mood, and adherence before escalating treatment. Retinoid-class products, oral tetracycline-class antibiotics, hormonal therapy, spironolactone, and isotretinoin each bring distinct reproductive, interaction, laboratory, or monitoring considerations.

Severe nodular acne, scarring, significant psychosocial impact, diagnostic uncertainty, or failure of an appropriately structured plan should trigger dermatology referral. Isotretinoin is not a casual “strong acne medicine”; it requires a regulated, medication-specific safety framework.

Part 7 — Psoriasis: Look Beyond the Plaque

Psoriasis is an immune-mediated condition that can involve skin, nails, joints, and important comorbidities. Well-demarcated plaques with scale may suggest psoriasis, but fungal disease, eczema, medication eruption, and other disorders remain in the differential. Ask about joint pain, morning stiffness, swollen digits, nail changes, functional limitation, and family history.

Topical therapies may be appropriate for limited disease. Extensive disease, genital/facial involvement, suspected psoriatic arthritis, erythroderma, severe flare, or inadequate response requires dermatology or rheumatology collaboration. Avoid reflexively prescribing systemic steroids for psoriasis without a disease-specific plan and specialty awareness.

Part 8 — Bacterial Skin Infection: Diagnose Purulence and Severity

Cellulitis is a clinical diagnosis characterized by warmth, tenderness, erythema, and swelling in deeper skin/subcutaneous tissue. It must be distinguished from abscess, dermatitis, venous stasis, lymphedema, deep venous thrombosis, necrotizing infection, and other mimics. Ask about trauma, skin breaks, edema, tinea pedis, injection drug use, bites, immune compromise, and systemic symptoms.

Purulent infection may need incision and drainage; nonpurulent cellulitis has a different empiric strategy. Culture is not routine for every uncomplicated cellulitis presentation, but may matter with severe systemic features, immune compromise, bites, immersion injuries, recurrent/atypical disease, or treatment failure. Choose antibiotics using local guidance, allergy history, renal/hepatic function, pregnancy context, severity, and likely pathogens—not habit.

Part 9 — Cellulitis Red Flags

Rapid spread, fever/chills, hypotension, severe pain out of proportion, bullae, skin necrosis, crepitus, altered mental status, or failure of appropriate outpatient treatment can indicate serious infection or an alternative diagnosis. Necrotizing soft-tissue infection is a surgical emergency; no outpatient antibiotic prescription makes that safe.

Marking borders, documenting vital signs and systemic findings, arranging a clear recheck, and giving return precautions are medication-safety actions. Treating without follow-up is not complete outpatient management.

Part 10 — Fungal Disease and the Steroid Trap

Tinea can be scaly, annular, pruritic, or atypical after steroid exposure. A topical corticosteroid can reduce redness while allowing fungal disease to spread or become less recognizable. When morphology and distribution suggest fungal disease, reassess the diagnosis and use appropriate testing or treatment rather than escalating steroid potency.

Foot and nail disease may act as a reservoir for recurrent lower-extremity skin infection. Addressing barrier disruption, tinea pedis, wounds, edema, and diabetes-related foot risk is part of preventing recurrent cellulitis.

Part 11 — Drug Eruptions: Medication Reconciliation Can Be Life-Saving

A new widespread rash should prompt a medication timeline that includes prescriptions, OTC medications, supplements, recent antibiotics, antiseizure medication changes, and intermittent agents. Ask about fever, facial swelling, mucosal lesions, skin pain, blistering, target lesions, lymphadenopathy, organ symptoms, and systemic illness.

Skin pain, blistering, mucosal involvement, fever, facial edema, hypotension, or systemic symptoms after a new medication can signal a severe cutaneous adverse reaction. This requires urgent/emergency assessment rather than home treatment with an antihistamine alone.

Part 12 — Clinical Case: “Eczema” That Is Getting Worse

A patient treated with a potent topical steroid reports rapidly expanding painful plaques with warmth, drainage, and fever.

FNP reasoning: reassess the diagnosis. Pain, warmth, drainage, and systemic symptoms raise concern for infection; increasing steroid potency without evaluation could delay proper care. Assess stability, examine for cellulitis/abscess or other infection, and determine urgency.

Part 13 — Clinical Case: Acne and Antibiotic Stewardship

A college student requests a third consecutive refill of an oral antibiotic for acne. They use no topical retinoid or benzoyl peroxide and now have intermittent diarrhea.

FNP reasoning: assess severity, scarring, adherence, adverse effects, pregnancy potential, other medications, and need for a multi-mechanism regimen or dermatology referral. Long, unstructured antibiotic exposure is not a complete acne plan.

Part 14 — Clinical Case: Pain Out of Proportion

A patient with diabetes has rapidly progressive leg erythema, severe pain exceeding the visible findings, fever, and new confusion.

FNP reasoning: this is not routine cellulitis. Severe systemic symptoms and pain out of proportion demand emergency evaluation for serious infection and other dangerous causes.

FNP Dermatologic Pharmacology Framework

  1. Describe lesions and distribution before naming the diagnosis.
  2. Screen for infection, severe drug reaction, mucosal disease, systemic illness, and high-risk host factors.
  3. Choose topical therapy by diagnosis, body site, vehicle, potency, duration, and patient ability to use it safely.
  4. Use antibiotics only with a clear indication, pathogen/severity logic, and reassessment plan.
  5. Consider pregnancy, immune status, drug interactions, kidney/liver function, and medication adverse effects.
  6. Refer or escalate for severe, widespread, refractory, scarring, joint-associated, atypical, or unstable disease.

High-Yield Summary

Topical corticosteroids: select carefully by diagnosis and body site; prolonged/high-potency misuse can damage skin.
Eczema: barrier care plus targeted anti-inflammatory therapy; worsening pain, crusting, fever, or erosions require reassessment for infection.
Acne: combine mechanisms and limit antibiotics; use benzoyl peroxide with antibiotic therapy when appropriate.
Cellulitis: distinguish purulent from nonpurulent disease and identify systemic or necrotizing red flags.
New rash after medication: fever, skin pain, blistering, or mucosal involvement is an emergency pattern.

Clinical safety note: This lesson is educational. Dermatologic diagnosis, medication selection, potency/duration decisions, antimicrobial prescribing, biopsy decisions, and emergency disposition must follow current guidelines, FDA-approved prescribing information, local scope requirements, and the individual patient’s clinical context.
